## Objectives

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em"}
- Define what concurrency is, and how it differs from parallelism.
- Define the different ways to handle multiple clients at the same time:
  - Multiprocessing.
  - Multithreading.
  - Asynchronous programming.
- Implement and manage concurrency in Java network applications.
- Choose between platform threads, thread pools and virtual threads.
:::

## Scope

- The concurrency a **network application** needs: several clients at the same
  time, data shared safely.
- A few classes of `java.util.concurrent`, the bare minimum.
- Other teaching units go deeper into concurrency.

# Concurrency: an introduction

## Concurrency and parallelism

- **Concurrency**: the execution of several tasks overlaps in time. A task can
  start without waiting for the others to finish.
  - A server accepts a new client while it serves the others.
- **Parallelism**: several tasks execute at the same instant, on different cores.
- On one core, concurrent tasks take turns; on several cores, they can also run in
  parallel.

**Concurrent does not always mean parallel.**

## What is a processor?

- Piece of hardware that executes billions of instructions every second.
- Also called CPU (Central Processing Unit).
- Processors can have one or multiple cores (single-core or multi-core
  processors).

## What is a core?

- A physical unit inside a processor that executes instructions.
- Simplified: each core executes one instruction, of one thread, at a time.
- With multiple processors and/or cores, the machine executes multiple
  instructions at the same time, one per core.

## What is a process?

- A program in execution, identified by a process ID.
- Each process has its own memory: by default, the other processes do not see
  it.
- Expensive to create and to destroy, compared to a thread.
- Processes communicate through the operating system (IPC): a socket on
  `localhost`, a pipe, a file, shared memory.

## What is a thread? (1/2)

- A sequence of instructions that runs inside a process, with its own stack.
- The main thread starts when the application starts; it can create other
  threads for other tasks.
- The operating system decides which thread runs on which core (scheduling):
  - On one core, it switches very quickly: they _appear_ to run together.
  - On several cores, they can really run at the same time.

## What is a thread? (2/2)

- The threads of a process **share its memory**.
- Much cheaper than processes, but the number of operating-system threads is
  limited.
- With threads, a server manages multiple clients at the same time: each client is
  handled by its own thread.

## What problems can concurrency cause?

- What happens when a client connects to the server?
- How to isolate the data sent by one client from the others?
- What happens when multiple clients want to access the same resource
  (variables) at the same time?

## What happens when multiple threads access the same resource?

- The operating system can switch between threads at any time, even in the middle
  of a Java statement; on several cores, two threads run at the same instant.
- The order in which the threads run is not guaranteed.
- `count++` is three steps: read, add one, write. Two threads that read the same
  value lose one increment.
- These problems are called **race conditions**.

# Handling multiple clients

## Handling one client at a time

An **iterative server** serves its clients one after the other, whatever its
number of threads:

1. Create a socket to listen to incoming connections.
2. Accept a client: a new socket for this client.
3. Serve the clients one after the other, each until it leaves.

Analogy: a hotline with a single operator. The next callers hear "please hold".

Simple, but the next client waits.

## Handling multiple clients at the same time

A **concurrent server** handles multiple clients at the same time, with:

- Multiprocessing.
- Multithreading.
- Asynchronous programming.

This course focuses on **multithreading**.

## Multiprocessing

- Create an entirely new process for each client.
- Heavier than threads; the processes communicate with IPC[^ipc].
- Isolated: when the process of one client crashes, the others go on (Apache can
  work this way).
- Analogy: a separate call centre for each caller, with its own building and
  phone system.

[^ipc]: Inter-process communication: processes exchange data through the operating
    system, with a socket on `localhost`, a pipe, a file or shared memory.

## Multithreading: one thread per client

- The main thread creates a new thread for each client.
- Cheaper to create than processes, and the threads share memory.
- Unlimited operating-system threads can exhaust the system.
- Analogy: a new operator and a new desk for each call, until the building is
  full; then calls fail.

## Multithreading: a fixed thread pool

- A fixed number of threads, reused from one client to the next.
- The number of threads stays under control.
- When all the threads are busy, the next clients wait.
- Analogy: a fixed number of operators; the other callers wait on hold.

## Asynchronous programming

- Handle multiple clients with a few threads, often a single one.
- A callback is called when a task is completed.
- Analogy: "leave your number, we will call you back". The caller does other
  things meanwhile.
- Out of scope but interesting to know! Node.js is a good example.

# Concurrency in Java

## A task

The work to do for one client, as an object that implements `Runnable` (`run()`)
or `Callable` (`call()`, which returns a value):

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em"}
```java
static class ClientHandler implements Runnable {
  private final Socket socket;

  public ClientHandler(Socket socket) {
    this.socket = socket;
  }

  @Override
  public void run() {
    // Read from and write to the socket of the client, then close it
  }
}
```
:::

- `run()` takes no parameters: the constructor receives what the task needs.

## Running a task on a thread

- Calling `run()` yourself runs it on the current thread, like any method.
- **By hand**, on a new thread (`Runnable` only):

  `new Thread(new ClientHandler(socket)).start();`

- **With an
  [`ExecutorService`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/ExecutorService.html)**,
  which manages the threads for you (`Runnable` or `Callable`):

  `executor.submit(new ClientHandler(socket));`

- [`Executors`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/Executors.html)
  creates the different executors, each with its pros and cons.

## In code: a server

```java
try (ServerSocket serverSocket = new ServerSocket(PORT);
    ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10)) {
  while (!serverSocket.isClosed()) {
    Socket clientSocket = serverSocket.accept();
    executor.submit(new ClientHandler(clientSocket));
  }
}
```

- `submit()` returns at once: the main thread goes back to `accept()`.
- A fixed pool of 10 threads: up to 10 clients at the same time, the others wait.

## Platform threads and virtual threads

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
- Java has two kinds of `Thread`:
  - **Platform thread**: backed by one operating-system thread.
  - **Virtual thread**: managed by the JVM, which runs many of them on a few
    platform threads (carrier threads).
- A virtual thread blocked on the network or on `sleep()` **unmounts** from its
  carrier thread: the carrier then runs another virtual thread.
- The JVM schedules the virtual threads on the carriers, the operating system
  the carriers on the cores.
- Since Java 21.
:::

## Platform threads: one thread each

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-height: 3.2
flowchart TB
    subgraph JVM["Java virtual machine"]
        P1[Platform thread 1]
        P2[Platform thread 2]
        P3[Platform thread 3]
    end
    subgraph OS["Operating system"]
        T1[Thread]
        T2[Thread]
        T3[Thread]
    end
    P1 --> T1
    P2 --> T2
    P3 --> T3
    style JVM fill:#f4f6f9,stroke:#8a94a6
    style OS fill:#f4f6f9,stroke:#8a94a6
```

- Each platform thread holds its own operating-system thread, blocked or not.

## Virtual threads: few carriers

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-height: 3.2
flowchart TB
    subgraph JVM["Java virtual machine"]
        V1[VT 1] & V2[VT 2] & V3[VT 3] --> C1[Carrier thread 1]
        V4[VT 4] & V5[VT 5] & V6[VT 6] --> C2[Carrier thread 2]
    end
    subgraph OS["Operating system"]
        T1[Thread]
        T2[Thread]
    end
    C1 --> T1
    C2 --> T2
    style JVM fill:#f4f6f9,stroke:#8a94a6
    style OS fill:#f4f6f9,stroke:#8a94a6
```

- A blocked virtual thread unmounts from its carrier thread: the carrier then runs
  another virtual thread.

## When to use virtual threads

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
- Fast to create, little memory: thousands, even millions, one per client.
- **Not faster, only lighter.**
- Useful when the tasks wait on the network: a network server.
- Pure computation: no better than a fixed pool of one thread per core.
- `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`: one virtual thread per task.
- Analogy: the operator puts a call on hold while waiting for a database, and
  takes another call. A few desks for many calls.
:::

# Sharing data between threads

## Ordinary variables are unsafe

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
- `int`, `HashMap`, `ArrayList`: wrong results when several threads change them
  at the same time (the race condition of `count++`).
- 8 threads, 100,000 `count++` each: `count` ends far below 800,000. A shared
  `HashMap` loses entries the same way.
- Two solutions:
  - **Locks**: one thread at a time runs a piece of code (not covered in this
    course).
  - **Thread-safe** types and data structures: their methods are atomic, several
    threads can call them at the same time.
:::

## Thread-safe variable types

- **Variable types** (`java.util.concurrent.atomic`):
  - `AtomicBoolean` instead of `boolean`/`Boolean`.
  - `AtomicInteger` instead of `int`/`Integer`.
  - `AtomicLong` instead of `long`/`Long`.

## Thread-safe data structures

- **Data structures** (`java.util.concurrent`):
  - `ConcurrentHashMap` instead of `HashMap`.
  - `CopyOnWriteArrayList` instead of `ArrayList`, when reads are much more
    frequent than writes (each write copies the list).
  - `CopyOnWriteArraySet` instead of `HashSet`, for small sets.
  - `ConcurrentLinkedQueue` instead of `LinkedList`.

## Several values together

- Most single calls (`incrementAndGet()`, `put()`) are atomic; two calls in a row
  are two operations.
- `containsKey()` then `put()`: two clients can take the same name.
  `putIfAbsent()` checks and takes it in one atomic operation (`null` if it was
  free).
- To update several values together, you need locks again.

# Go further

## Benchmark

::: {style="font-size: 0.6em"}
1,000 connections at once. Requests per second, Linux, Java 25, 14 cores:

| Server | `SLEEP` (wait 100 ms) | `COMPUTE` (about 6 ms) |
|---|---:|---:|
| `single` (iterative) | 10 | 170 to 175 |
| `thread` (one platform thread per client) | 2,300 to 2,800 | 1,200 to 1,300 |
| `cached` | 2,800 to 3,000 | 1,400 |
| `fixed-4` | 39 | 655 to 673 |
| `fixed-14` (one thread per core) | 134 | 1,310 to 1,530 |
| `fixed-500` | 2,400 to 2,600 | 1,360 |
| `virtual` | 4,500 to 5,800 | 1,330 to 1,500 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[50,25,25]"}
:::

- Waiting: every 100 ms, a fixed pool handles as many requests as it has threads.
- Computing: the cores limit the work.

## What will you do?

- Run the servers with several clients at the same time, and see how each one
  handles them.
- Answer questions about the different strategies.
